_about: Learn hub lessons, written by Claude. Mechanics only: how things work, never which way a currency will go. No figures that go stale; live numbers come from the site's own data.

lessons.title: What moves a currency
lessons.lead: A currency is the price of one country's money in terms of another's. It rises when more people want to hold it and falls when fewer do.

sections.p: Money goes where it is paid and where it feels safe. Higher interest rates pay more for holding a currency. A growing economy draws investment. In nervous markets, money runs to a few currencies seen as safe.
No currency is strong on its own. The dollar can have good news and still fall against the pound if Britain's news is better. Every question about a currency is really a question about two.
Markets trade on what they expect, not on what has happened. A rate rise that everyone saw coming is already in the price. What moves a currency is news that changes the outlook.

Blue Street sorts the evidence into seven drivers: policy, growth, inflation, risk sentiment, terms of trade, positioning and fiscal health. Each has its own lesson. Together they make the case for or against a currency.

lessons.title: How to read a data release
lessons.lead: A data release is a scheduled number about an economy, such as inflation or jobs. The number matters less than how it compares with what was expected.

sections.p: Every release has a forecast, a result and the last reading. The forecast is what economists expected. The result is what came out. The last reading shows the direction of travel.

sections.h: The surprise is what moves things
sections.p: Markets price in the forecast before the release. If the result matches, little happens. If it beats or misses by a wide margin, traders rethink what the central bank will do next, and the currency moves.

sections.h: Good news is not always good
sections.p: A strong number usually helps a currency because it points to higher rates. For some numbers, lower is better: a falling unemployment rate is a beat. Blue Street marks each result as beat or missed for the currency, so you do not have to work it out.
Last month's number is often changed when the new one comes out. A strong result with a big downward revision can amount to a weak report. One release rarely changes the story. A run of them does.

lessons.title: How to build a view
lessons.lead: A view is your own judgment of where a currency is heading and why. Blue Street lays out the evidence. The judgment is yours.

sections.p: Read what is driving the currency right now. Which of the seven drivers are helping it, and which are holding it back? If you cannot say it in a sentence, you do not have a view yet.

sections.h: Then look at the other side
sections.p: You trade a pair, so do the same for the second currency. The clearest cases pair a currency with a lot going for it against one with a lot going against it.

Every view rests on a few things staying true. Name them. Then look at the calendar for the events that could break them. A view with a big event tomorrow is a different thing from one with a quiet week ahead.

Fundamentals play out over weeks and months. Day to day, prices also move on surprises, positioning and noise. A sound view can lose money for a while. The fundamentals tell you which way to lean, not when to act.

lessons.title: Policy: what the central bank does with rates
lessons.lead: Policy is the central bank's interest rate and where it is heading next. It is the driver that matters most, most of the time.

sections.p: Each central bank sets a short-term interest rate for its economy. It raises the rate to cool inflation and cuts it to support growth. Markets also watch what the bank says about its next moves.

A higher rate pays more to anyone holding that currency. Money flows toward better returns, and that demand lifts the currency. What counts is the gap between two countries' rates and which way that gap is moving.

Rate decisions, the statement and press conference that follow, speeches by officials, and the minutes of past meetings. Also watch what markets expect: Blue Street tells you whether a move is already expected.
A rate rise does not always lift a currency. If it was fully expected, or the bank hints it is the last one, the currency can fall on the day. The surprise and the outlook matter more than the move.

lessons.title: Growth: how strong the economy looks
lessons.lead: Growth is how fast an economy is expanding and how healthy its job market is.

sections.p: The size of the economy, measured by GDP, plus the signs that show up sooner: jobs, wages, shop sales, factory output and business surveys.
A strong economy attracts investment and gives the central bank room to keep rates higher. A weak one does the opposite. Growth mostly works through what it means for rates.
Jobs reports, retail sales, business surveys and GDP. Because every country reports on its own schedule, the useful question is which economy is doing better than expected right now.
Growth numbers look backward. GDP tells you about a quarter that ended weeks ago. Surveys and jobs data are fresher, so they often move markets more.

lessons.title: Inflation: how fast prices are rising
lessons.lead: Inflation is the pace at which prices rise. Central banks aim to keep it low and steady, usually near 2% a year.

sections.p: The yearly change in the price of what households buy. Core inflation leaves out food and energy, which swing a lot, to show the underlying trend.

Inflation matters through the central bank. If prices rise too fast and the bank responds by raising rates, the currency tends to gain. If the bank does not respond, rising prices eat away at the currency's value and it tends to fall.
The monthly inflation report in each country, wage growth, and what people expect inflation to be. Compare each with the bank's goal.
High inflation is not good or bad for a currency on its own. Always ask the second question: what will the central bank do about it?

lessons.title: Risk sentiment: calm or nervous markets
lessons.lead: Risk sentiment is the mood of global markets: whether investors are reaching for returns or running for safety.

sections.p: In calm times investors buy things that pay more but can fall hard, such as shares. When something frightens them, they sell those and move into what feels safe.

Some currencies are treated as shelters. The yen, the Swiss franc and the US dollar tend to gain when markets are nervous. The Australian, New Zealand and Canadian dollars tend to gain when markets are calm and lose when they are not.
Stock markets, especially sharp falls. Wars, political shocks and banking trouble. A sudden change in mood can outweigh every other driver for days.
The usual pattern can break. If higher US rates are what is frightening markets, the dollar may rise while the yen and franc get little help.

lessons.title: Terms of trade: what a country sells and buys
lessons.lead: Terms of trade compare the prices of what a country exports with the prices of what it imports.

sections.p: Some countries sell a lot of raw materials. Canada sells oil. Australia sells iron ore, coal and gold. New Zealand sells dairy. Others, such as Japan and the euro area, buy most of their energy from abroad.
When export prices rise, more money flows into the country and its currency tends to gain. When import prices rise, more flows out. Dearer oil helps the Canadian dollar and hurts the yen.
Oil, gold, iron ore and dairy prices, and demand from China, the biggest buyer of many raw materials.
The link is not instant or exact. A commodity can rise for a reason that hurts the exporter too, such as a war that also frightens markets.

lessons.title: Positioning: how traders are already placed
lessons.lead: Positioning shows how large traders have already bet on a currency. It tells you who is left to buy or sell.

sections.p: Once a week the US futures regulator publishes how big groups of traders are placed. Blue Street follows two: hedge funds, which move fast, and real money managers such as pension funds, which move slowly.
A trend needs new buyers. When nearly everyone who wants to bet on a currency already has, there are few left to push it further. A small disappointment can then cause a sharp move the other way.
How large the bet is compared with its own history, and whether hedge funds and real money agree. A bet near the largest in ten years deserves attention.
An extreme bet is a warning, not a signal. Lopsided positioning can stay lopsided for months while the price keeps going.

lessons.title: Fiscal health: government borrowing and debt
lessons.lead: Fiscal health is how much a government spends compared with what it collects, and how much it owes.

sections.p: When a government spends more than it takes in, it borrows by selling bonds. Investors decide what interest they want for lending to it.
Most of the time it sits in the background. It comes forward when investors start to doubt a government's finances. They demand more interest, or sell the bonds and the currency together.
Budgets, borrowing figures, bond sales that draw weak demand, and the gap between one country's borrowing costs and a safer neighbour's.
Higher bond yields are not always good for a currency. Yields rising because the economy is strong help it. Yields rising because lenders are worried do not.

lessons.title: Inflation reports
lessons.lead: The monthly inflation report shows how fast consumer prices are rising. It is one of the two releases that move currencies most.

sections.p: The change in prices over the month and the year. The headline figure covers everything. The core figure leaves out food and energy.
It is the number the central bank is trying to control. A higher result than forecast raises the odds of higher rates, which tends to help the currency. A lower one does the reverse.
Look at core first, and at the monthly change before the yearly one. The yearly figure can move just because of what happened twelve months ago.
In the US there are two measures. The consumer price index comes out first and moves markets most. The Federal Reserve's own goal is set on a second measure that comes out later in the month.

lessons.title: Jobs reports
lessons.lead: A jobs report counts how many people found or lost work, how many are unemployed, and how fast pay is rising.

sections.p: Three things: the number of jobs added, the unemployment rate, and wage growth. The US report comes out on the first Friday of most months and is the most watched release in the world.
Jobs tell a central bank how hot the economy is running. Strong hiring and fast pay rises point to higher rates. Rising unemployment points to lower ones.
Do not stop at the headline. A big jobs number with slowing pay and a higher unemployment rate is a mixed report. Check the changes to the previous two months as well.
For the unemployment rate, lower is better for the currency. Blue Street marks each result as beat or missed so the direction is clear.

lessons.title: Growth figures: GDP and retail sales
lessons.lead: GDP measures the size of the whole economy. Retail sales measure what shoppers spent. Both show whether an economy is speeding up or slowing down.

sections.p: GDP comes out every quarter, often in more than one version as more information arrives. Retail sales come out every month and are much fresher.
Faster growth supports higher rates and draws investment. Slower growth does the opposite.
GDP is old news by the time it lands, so it moves markets only when it surprises. Retail sales are jumpy from month to month, so look at a few months together.
Some countries report growth compared with the quarter before, and some turn that into a yearly pace. Check which one you are looking at before comparing two countries.

lessons.title: Business surveys
lessons.lead: A business survey asks company managers whether things are getting better or worse. It is the earliest read on an economy each month.

sections.p: Managers report on orders, output, hiring and prices. The answers are turned into one number. For the most common kind, above 50 means business is expanding and below 50 means it is shrinking.
They arrive weeks before the official figures, so they are the first sign of a turn. A sharp move in a survey often shows up in jobs and growth data later.
Watch the direction and the 50 line. Look inside too: the parts on new orders, hiring and prices paid often say more than the headline.
There are separate surveys for factories and for services. In most rich economies services are much the larger part.

lessons.title: Rate decisions and the words around them
lessons.lead: A rate decision is the day a central bank announces whether it is raising, cutting or holding its interest rate.

sections.p: The bank publishes its decision and a statement. Many hold a press conference soon after. Some also publish forecasts, and most release the minutes of the meeting a few weeks later.

The decision itself is usually expected. The currency moves on anything that changes the outlook: the wording of the statement, how the votes split, the forecasts, and how the head of the bank answers questions.
Ask three things. Was the decision expected? Did the bank sound more or less likely to move again? Did anyone vote against? A bank can raise rates and weaken its currency by hinting it is finished.
Speeches between meetings matter for the same reason. Officials use them to steer expectations, so that the decision day holds no shock.

lessons.title: What a central bank does
lessons.lead: A central bank manages a country's money. Its main job is to keep prices steady, and its main tool is the interest rate.

sections.p: Most central banks aim for inflation of about 2% a year. Some, like the US Federal Reserve, are also told to keep as many people in work as possible.
The bank sets the rate at which commercial banks borrow for very short periods. That rate feeds into mortgages, business loans and savings rates across the economy.
A bank can buy or sell bonds to push longer-term rates down or up. A few, notably in Switzerland and Japan, sometimes buy or sell their own currency directly to move its price.
A bank that leans toward higher rates is called hawkish. One that leans toward lower rates is called dovish. Blue Street labels each bank one of the two, or neutral, and says why.

lessons.title: The eight central banks
lessons.lead: Eight central banks stand behind the eight major currencies. They share a goal but differ in how they pursue it.

sections.p: Two goals: steady prices, with inflation at 2%, and as many people in work as possible. It sets a range for its rate, not a single number, and meets eight times a year.
One goal: inflation at 2% over the medium term, for every country that uses the euro. It sets several rates. The one markets follow is what it pays banks on deposits.
Inflation at 2%, a target set by the government. Nine people vote, and how the votes split is published. A close vote is news in itself.
Inflation at 2%, after decades when prices barely rose. Its rates have long been the lowest of the eight, which is why the yen is so sensitive to rates elsewhere.
Inflation between 0% and 2%. It meets only four times a year, and it is willing to buy or sell francs to stop the currency getting too strong or too weak.
Inflation at 2%, the middle of a band from 1% to 3%. The economy is closely tied to the US and to the price of oil.
Inflation between 2% and 3%, and full employment. The economy leans on exports of raw materials, much of them to China.

sections.h: Reserve Bank of New Zealand (New Zealand dollar)
sections.p: Inflation between 1% and 3%, aiming for the middle. A small, open economy, so its currency often moves with global mood and dairy prices.

lessons.title: How the strength score works
lessons.lead: The strength score sums up how much of the evidence is working for or against a currency right now.

sections.p: Each of the seven drivers gets a mark for each currency: plus one if it supports the currency, minus one if it weighs on it, zero if it is doing little. The score is the total.
Use it to see at a glance which currencies have the most going for them, then open the currency's page to read why. The reasons matter more than the number.
It is not a forecast and not a signal to trade. A currency with a high score can fall for weeks. The score describes the fundamentals, which work slowly.

lessons.title: How to use the pair picker
lessons.lead: The pair picker starts from your view on one currency and shows which pairs fit it best.

sections.p: Say whether you are bullish or bearish on a currency. The picker compares it with each of the other seven and ranks the pairs by the gap between the two scores.
Why the other currency is strong or weak, what holding the pair pays or costs in interest each year, and the next big event that could move it.
The top pairs are where the evidence is most one-sided. Check the next event before anything else. The picker gives evidence for a view. It never tells you to trade.

lessons.title: How to read the Positioning page
lessons.lead: The Positioning page shows what large traders have already bet on each currency, gold and oil.

sections.p: Hedge funds trade fast and follow trends. Real money managers, such as pension funds, move slowly and often hedge. Each gets its own dot on the line.
The left end means betting against, the middle means even, the right end means betting for. The further a dot sits from the middle, the bigger the bet.
A bet close to its largest since 2015, and places where the two groups disagree. Both are flagged for you. The figures come out once a week and are a few days old when they arrive.
